newsitem.title: FRANCE: French unions oppose labour market "flexibility".
newsitem.headline: French unions oppose labour market "flexibility".

text.p: French trade unions urged Labour Minister Jacques Barrot on Thursday to ignore bosses' calls to make it easier to hire and fire workers and criticised a proposed youth job training scheme.

"There's already enough (labour market) flexibility. Everyone knows the idea of the disposable employee," said Alain Deleu, head of the moderate CFTC union after talks with Barrot on ways to combat record 12.7 percent unemployment.

In talks with a succession of union leaders, Barrot sought to calm their fears that the centre-right government wanted to bulldoze through proposals by the CNPF employers' federation to make the labour market more flexible.
Barrot also sought to reassure unions that a youth job training scheme proposed by employers was not a bid to revive a sub-minimum wage for the young.

The CNPF argues that industrialists would be more willing to create jobs if it was easier to shed staff in times of economic difficulty. Unions say such "flexibility" would lead to what they reckon are too harsh U.S. or British labour practices.

"It's a false idea" that labour laws are too rigid in France, said Nicole Notat, head of the pro-Socialist CFDT union. She urged Barrot to appoint an independent investigator to study French labour laws.
Louis Viannet, head of the Communist-led CGT union, said that even though Barrot "doesn't want to use the word 'flexibility', (his) lines of reflection...follow those of the CNPF."

But he said Barrot was "fairly prudent" about how to follow up the employers' proposals. Deleu also said Barrot seemed to want to avoid legislating and was encouraging dialogue between bosses and unions.

Marc Blondel, secretary-general of the Force Ouvriere (FO) union, said he asked President Jacques Chirac about the plan by employers for work training leading to a diploma in exchange for 1,500 francs ($283) a month, one-quarter of the minimum wage.

He compared the scheme, touted by Chirac last month as a key initiative to combat one-in-four youth unemployment, to a bid by ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur in 1994 to introduce a lower minimum wage for young people on work experience.
Balladur's scheme was scrapped after huge student protests.

Viannet, whose union spearheaded a crippling 24-day public sector strike in 1995 alongside Blondel's FO, said he felt slightly reassured after meeting Barrot that the government did not want to revive Balladur's scheme.

He said Barrot wanted training to be part of a university course, rather than after it. "That fairly substantially modifies the fears and criticisms that we have expressed," he said, but added it did not resolve all problems.
